What about Supper After Dark: Roman Taverns and Food?

You stand on this shop street in Rome while evening air carries warm stew and the damp of stone. Footsteps slow as people leave their labour and turn toward food. Long custom already gives the main meal a name of its own. People call that sitting the cena. What about Wheels in the Dark: Night Traffic in Ancient Rome?

You stand in a side street of Rome on a cool night in Trajan's reign. High walls hold the air, and a loaded cart meets the uneven paving. One wheel gives a low click. Farther along, a drover calls to his animals under windows where households are trying to rest. Trade that waited through the bright hours rolls in now, sack by sack and jar by jar. What about Cock-Crow and the Bakers?

You hear the upper stone before the yard comes into view. Warm meal smells of wheat in the cool air. This is a bakery yard in Rome, in the reign of Trajan, while cock-crow is only starting. Custom places the breakfast called ientaculum at dawn, so the mill has been turning for hours. The pistores, the professional bakers, grind now so renters can buy bread instead of baking every loaf at home. What about Dawn at the Door: The Morning Call on a Patron?

Cold stone meets your sandals at a patron's doorway, and the air still holds the damp of the night. Grey light finds the threshold before the street has warmed. This is dawn in Rome, outside a patron's house, in the reign of the emperor Trajan. Clients have gathered for the daily morning reception in his house, called the salutatio, each one bringing a request meant for this early hour. Rank sets the order as the first light makes the gathering plain to anyone passing in the street.

00:00Intro · 393 words

The Romans did not have one word for the night. They had a name for every part of it, from vespera, the evening just after sunset, to gallicinium, when the cocks began to crow.

Tonight, I'll walk you through each of those hours in Trajan's Rome, until the bakers pull the first loaves from their ovens at dawn.

This is Dreaming Ages.

We blend rich historical research with a slow, calming narration, soothing music, and immersive night sounds. Our stories offer just enough history to engage your mind without keeping it awake, easing you into a natural slumber. Don't worry about making it to the end; you can always pick up where you left off tomorrow. Tonight, wrap yourself in the comfort of a slow-paced story, the gentle glow of a clay lamp, and water running in a stone street fountain.

Now… pull up the blanket, and rest your head on the pillow.

Let's begin with a few slow breaths in… and some long breaths out. Feel your shoulders soften, and let each breath settle a little deeper than the last. There's nowhere you need to be tonight, and nothing more to be done.

I'll blow out the candle… Now… follow me back in time, to lamplight, tiled roofs, and a fountain that never stops running.

It's an evening in early autumn, in the year one hundred and thirteen, in the city of Rome, while the emperor Trajan rules. The heat is going out of the paving stones, and on a street corner below the Quirinal Hill, water spills from a stone spout into a wide basin, as it does all day and all night. Above the roofs, the first star of evening is out over the hills.

The city, its laws and its writers are real, and the facts tonight come from the record. The few ordinary people with names are imagined, but people very like them lived in these streets.

Night was a row of named moments, and that is what the named stretches of the night meant to people who kept no one dial in the dark. Each stretch told you where the hours after sunset had got to. A name was enough. Bedtime was not the same quiet as the dead of night, and cock-crow was not the same quiet as the hush that followed it, so work could wait or go on by the name alone.

Romans numbered the hours as well, and a night hour could be called prima noctis hora, the first hour of the night. Later hours followed. The twelfth belonged only to its own light or its own dark, and the count began again when the sun rose or set.

Because day and night changed with the seasons, the length of the Roman hour changed too. Romans knew that daytime length depended on latitude as well as on the season, so the same count did not fit every city under the same sky.

Historians put the city, through the first and second centuries, at about one million people, and that figure is a conventional estimate rather than a census count.

No reliable records survive for the general demography of the empire, so a careful total of heads stays out of reach. Writers of the age liked a strong tale more than a measured count. Scholars find moralizing and anecdotal remarks of little use for studying the population. Housing is the firmer ground under your feet tonight, closer to what can be walked than any sum of names.

Insulae, the rented apartment blocks of the early imperial years, house most of the urban citizen population of that huge city. An insula lets an ordinary household take a room on the same streets as wealthier neighbours. Trade keeps a shop on the ground floor, with beds rising in storeys over the counters. Families carry supper upward once the selling stops, each bundle meant for a different landing.

Plebeians live upstairs, ordinary people of lower or middle standing in the city's daily life. Some of the equites, a prosperous order of citizens, live in insulae as well, though the richest of them keep a private house. A clerk might share the climb with a craftsman. Someone of substantial means can hold the next door, and the three purses never match, though the block around them is one rented building.

Traditional elite households and the very wealthy keep a domus, a large single-family house, often set around its own court. Tabernae fill the ground floor of an insula, shops and small businesses set into the front, with living space beginning overhead. Heat from the pot warms the front of the counter, and a strip of linen keeps the flies off the dishes. Julia's sleeves are rolled to the elbow. Steam beads on the clay. She counts the last coins into a wooden box, then slides the box under the board where her hand can find it in the dim.

Imagine the landing just above her shop. Felix, her neighbour, comes up with a loaf under one arm and a jug in the other hand, and the timber answers each step. His key finds the lock. Several people can own one insula together, while each resident still pays rent to keep a single room. Some insulae, not every block in the city, were put up at minimal expense for speculation, and the construction suffered for the saving. After that earlier cap, Trajan reduced the allowed height to sixty Roman feet, about seventeen and three quarters metres. From one hundred and twenty-three before the common era, citizens could buy a monthly grain ration at a fixed low price. The ration, called the frumentatio, was unmilled wheat, as much as thirty-three kilograms. It arrived whole. Someone still had to grind and bake it before a renter could eat, which is why these stones turn in the dark. The pistores take that public share and work it toward the morning loaf.

In fifty-eight before the common era the tribune Publius Clodius Pulcher abolished the charge for the grain. Citizens could then draw the monthly wheat without paying for it. Titus shifts a sack that came in on the night carts, when heavy wheels were allowed through the streets. He loosens the neck and lets the wheat run toward the stone. Cool yard air meets warmer air off the oven wall as he leans to the sack.

Bakeries commonly used slaves or criminals as workers at the stones and the ovens. Imagine those workers turning the upper stone in the dark, feet braced on packed earth. Titus pushes a wooden bar, and warm meal spills at the rim until the bin fills. He shakes his wrist when a second man takes the bar from him. The scrape stays even under the new hands, and the bin rises in a soft heap.

Pliny the Elder says women were the main bakers in most families, though that rests on his writing rather than a shop count. Many homes still kept their own loaves beside the professional trade. A rented room might hold a small bake for the people who lived there. Lucius passes with a jar filled at the street fountain, where the bakers draw their water. He tips it in, and the meal takes the water with a soft slap.

Under Trajan a collegium pistorum, a bakers' college, is said to have been set up so the bread supply would not fail. The report is not certain. Lucius sets the jar by the wall and turns back across the damp ground for another fill. He will need that second jar before the dough is wet enough to hold its shape. A thin run of water still moves in the channel beside the path he takes.

At cock-crow the new civil day is already hours old, though the sky has not lightened. The mill has been turning inside that new day for some time already. Cocks call from a roof beyond the wall, one voice and then another. Titus keeps the bar moving so the meal stays fine enough for the trough. Flour lies light on the board where the next round will be shaped by hand.

Bakers named their tools the fornax, the testum, the thermospodium, and the clibanus. The testum served as a portable oven, so a batch could leave the fixed hearth. Imagine a worker setting that cover on a clear patch of floor, with meal piled beside it. He seats it over a round and leaves the dough to take the heat. Then he turns back to the trough, where the next mass is still being worked by hand.

Archaeologists have found more than thirty commercial bakeries in Pompeii. When that city was destroyed in the year seventy-nine, at least thirty-three bakeries were still in use. What remains in those shops shows how far the professional trade had spread by then. A mill, a counter, and an oven mark the same craft you are watching in this yard. This yard keeps those same hours, with meal on the board and water waiting in the trough.

The tomb inscription names its owner, Marcus Vergilius, as baker, contractor, and public servant. His last Latin title is still debated in translation, so the exact office stays unsure. He belongs to the end of the Republic, long before this yard's own night. His surviving tomb, later overshadowed by the Aqua Claudia, stands about seven metres high. Those titles keep a baker's public work in view while the stones here keep turning.

Martial, writing around the year one hundred, complains that a poor man in Rome cannot find quiet. Schoolmasters fill the morning, and corn grinders work at night. The bar knocks once. Then it settles into a steady scrape as Titus shifts his grip on the wood. Another worker folds the mix with a wooden scoop until the mass holds a clean swirl.

You are still beside the mill, and the second cock has not finished its call. Someone lifts the cover from a small testum that has finished on a round. Steam leaves the crust, and he taps it once with a knuckle to judge the bake. He slides the round onto a wooden board and sets the board on the shelf by the counter. A buyer will be able to take it at dawn without having mixed the dough at home.

Lucius returns with the second jar and pours until the mix leaves the sides of the trough. The meal darkens as it drinks, and a scoop presses until the mass holds together. Cocks answer each other from two roofs, the later call crossing the first. Hands shape a round and set it near the warm oven wall to wait its turn. A fresh sack sits within reach of the bar, and the slow circle of the stone does not break.

Renters upstairs do not keep a full kitchen for every loaf, so they buy what the night has made. That trade is what the pistores opened for a city of rented rooms. A woman with a wrap over her arm waits near the counter, though the street is still dim. She has come early because the ientaculum comes with the first light of day. Two rounds already sit on the shelf, and a third is still under its cover on the floor.

Around you the yard sits between tall walls and a street still dim. Grain that left the public store as whole wheat is meal now, pale and warm at the stone's rim. Titus brushes a little into the bin with the side of his hand. His palm comes away pale, and he wipes it on his tunic before taking the bar again. The upper stone answers with the low scrape it has kept since well before the first cock.

Outside the gate the street is a strip of packed earth between tall buildings. Someone in an upper room coughs once, and then the lane is quiet again. The fountain down the lane still runs, the same flow the jar was filled from earlier. Lucius rinses his hands in the channel and shakes them dry over the dirt floor. He steps back to the trough, where the dough has begun to pull cleanly away from the wood.

He sets the wooden bar aside where the next man can take it without a search. Meal still warm in the bin will go into the next trough when the water is ready. A cover rests on the testum, and the crust beneath has finished taking the heat. The man by the oven slides that round onto the shelf and reaches for another cover. Cock-crow has passed, and the street beyond the gate is taking on a paler colour.

The pistores turn the public wheat through the night so that bread is ready by cock-crow, and a renter can buy what a small room cannot bake. That night grinding is what lets a city of rented rooms eat when the day begins. The millstone slows, and then it comes to a stop.

1:30:08Dawn at the Door: The Morning Call on a Patron · 1,538 words

Cold stone meets your sandals at a patron's doorway, and the air still holds the damp of the night. Grey light finds the threshold before the street has warmed. This is dawn in Rome, outside a patron's house, in the reign of the emperor Trajan. Clients have gathered for the daily morning reception in his house, called the salutatio, each one bringing a request meant for this early hour. Rank sets the order as the first light makes the gathering plain to anyone passing in the street.

Clemens has come with the others, a warm loaf from the bakery under one arm and a folded tablet in his hand. He wants a hearing, the ordinary ask of this hour, before errands pull people apart. Someone coughs into a sleeve when the door opens again. Cold air slips across the floor. You feel shoulders press as the court fills and a chair is set for the patron near the far wall.

Inside, he receives them at dawn in the atrium, the open court of the house, and in the tablinum, the room where household papers are kept. A young man in a plain tunic sets a cup of water near the patron's hand and steps back at once. A table stands ready there, with a stool drawn up and a chest shut beside it. Clemens edges closer, the tablet still unopened, waiting for his turn in the line. The patron listens, nods once, and sends one client on before the line moves again.

Roman custom ranked the bond between patron and client, yet both sides owed something to the other. A client could ask. A patron owed a hearing, and he gained people willing to walk out with him when the greeting was done. That shared duty is what the salutatio carried from the private court into the public morning. Your place stays near the back, where the cool of the paved court has not yet lifted from the stone.

After the greeting, clients walk with the patron to the forum, and a large crowd of them is read as a sign of his standing. Imagine the doorway just then. Cloaks settle on shoulders, a few quiet words pass, and feet turn from the court toward the street. Private talk becomes a walk the neighbours can count as the company leaves the house. Sandals find the ruts and the smoother strips by turns while the doorway falls behind.

A strap is fixed as the line keeps a steady pace in the cool air. Clemens tucks the tablet inside his cloak when water drips from an overhang, and he keeps the loaf close so the crust will not cool. You hear feet more than voices, a soft repeated tap that carries the company on past shuttered shops. Farther along the street the men of the watch are going off duty, their night rounds finished, while your group keeps on toward the squares. A cart stands empty at a corner, its traces slack, and no one calls the group to hurry.

The walk brings you to Trajan's Forum, the last of the imperial fora built in ancient Rome. The emperor Trajan ordered it paid for with spoils from the conquest of Dacia, the wealth taken in that campaign, so a finished war lies under this paving. That conquest ended in one hundred and six. Construction began between one hundred and five and one hundred and seven, while crews were already promised to the site. By this dawn the complex has stood open since a calendar carved at Ostia dates its inauguration to one hundred and twelve.

Trajan's architect, a man from Damascus, oversaw the building, and his plan set a great portico-lined piazza, an open court edged with covered walks, at the heart of the work. The whole forum complex measured about three hundred metres long and one hundred and eighty-five metres wide, around that court, and the measure belongs to the full complex rather than to the open floor alone. Porticoes run along the measured ground. When your group comes through, the scale is what the architect left for a patron to cross with his clients in full view. Pale stone takes the thin light, and each step sounds a little clearer than it did in the street.

Workers removed a ridge that had joined the Quirinal and Capitoline hills, so the forum could sit on level ground between them. More than three hundred thousand cubic metres of soil and rock were dug out for the complex. Carts carried that load outside the Porta Collina, the Colline Gate, and left it beyond the wall. You come in with the others, sandals quiet on the new paving, and the patron does not slow until the whole company is through the entrance. The cut ground is only a memory under the marble, while the early air still smells faintly of damp stone.

The main way in was a triumphal arch at the south, made to recall the Dacian Wars for anyone entering. Beyond it the open space was paved entirely in Carrara marble, pale from colonnade to colonnade. Along the north side stood the Basilica Ulpia, broad enough for the public business of the morning. Imagine that wide floor. Clients cross it beside their patron, and the long porticoes make each figure look small before the hall.

You pause a moment under a portico while the patron greets a man who has walked at his side since the house. The clasp of hands is brief, and both turn back toward the open floor. A breeze passes along the marble. Clemens checks the tie on his tablet and shifts the loaf to his other arm so the crust will not mark his sleeve. Somewhere in the hall a wooden bench gives a small scrape, and the sound says the morning's business is near.

Trajan's Column was completed and dedicated on 12 May in one hundred and thirteen. The height given here is thirty-eight metres, though other passages give slightly different heights for the same monument. It stands between the two libraries, and from the paving you can follow the shaft upward against the paling sky. Those libraries keep state papers, including emperors' acts and praetors' edicts, ready for officials who would need them later in the day. Clemens keeps his eyes on the patron's shoulder so he will not miss a summons if his name is called.

Archaeologists still argue over both the place and the very existence of a temple of the deified Trajan at the far north. The question stays unsettled beyond the libraries, and no one in the line tries to settle it. Clemens stands half a step behind the patron, eyes on the open square, his request close at hand until he is called. By the time the group settles, the pace from the house has eased into a quiet tread across the wide floor. Under the southern arch the air is cooler, and footsteps pick up a hollow note as cloaks brush the stone.

Light lies in a soft sheet between the porticoes once you are through the passage again. Fingers shift a tablet from one hand to the other as the patron slows his step near the shade. A second client comes up from the rear and falls in beside him, speaking low, then falls silent when a third man joins them. You shift your weight, and the cool of the paving comes up through your sandals while the group waits. The column's base stays in shadow a little longer than the open marble, and a bird crosses high overhead before anyone speaks of it.

The group begins to loosen as errands draw one client, then another, toward the Basilica Ulpia. One man peels away with a nod, his errand already clear, and voices drop a little as he goes. Another stays, hoping the morning will still hold a place for his request, the tablet a small hard shape under his arm. Steps fade slowly across the Carrara floor. Morning business can take them into that hall when the patron gives the word, while the air around the column barely stirs.

Long after this night, the revived Aqua Virgo, called the Acqua Vergine, still ends at the Trevi Fountain, and that fountain marks the close of an aqueduct that once supplied ancient Rome. It is still thought to give some of Rome's purest drinking water. The water keeps arriving there, cool over stone, in a city whose doorways no longer fill at this hour with clients and tablets. A thin sound of falling water would be the only likeness left, steady and plain. Far from that later basin, this morning's company still stands on the pale paving of the forum.

The salutatio turned a private bond into a public walk at dawn, so a client could bring a request and a patron could show his standing by the size of the company around him. That morning custom gave both sides a place in the day, one asking and one seen, before the forum took the walk into its marble court. First sunlight touches the top of the Column while Clemens holds his place on the paving below.

1:41:03Goodnight in Rome · 307 words

Tonight, we've been a long way. The night began with its names, as the evening star came out over the roofs. Then came the insulae, the crowded apartment blocks, the aqueduct water spilling into the street basins, and the first oil lamps being lit. After a late supper, the carts rolled in under the daytime cart ban, and the vigiles walked by with their buckets. At midnight the Roman civil day turned, the pistores ground their grain at cock-crow, and at dawn the clients gathered for the salutatio. Some of that night is still here: a new date still begins in the middle of the night, just as the Roman civil day began, and the water of the Aqua Virgo still runs into the Trevi Fountain. All night long, the city kept working while it slept.

Now, it's time to rest. The carts have gone quiet at the gates, and the watchmen have set down their buckets for another night. In a bakery yard across the city, the pistores have swept the mill floor, and a lump of sourdough sits under a cloth, saved to raise tomorrow's bread, as Roman bakers had done since the Greek bakers came nearly three centuries before. And in Trajan's Forum the new column stands in the last of the dark, its carved band of the Dacian wars winding up out of sight, waiting for the light that will bring the clients out to their patrons' doors.

You don't need to do anything now. Nothing to remember. Nothing to finish. You can let the day go, the way water slips over the lip of a fountain and runs on into the dark. The roofs are dark. The stars turn slowly over the seven hills. And the water keeps running, soft and steady, all through the night.

Goodnight. Until next time, sleep well.
